[Education in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Canada "Education in Canada") is for the most part provided [publicly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_school "State school"), funded and overseen by [federal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Canada "Government of Canada"), [provincial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_and_territories_of_Canada "Provinces and territories of Canada"), and [local governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_government "Local government").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-84) Education is within provincial jurisdiction and the curriculum is overseen by the province.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-86) Education in Canada is generally divided into [primary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_education "Primary education"), followed by secondary education and post-secondary. Education in both English and French is available in most places across Canada.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-87) Canada has a large number of universities, almost all of which are publicly funded.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-88) Established in 1663, [Université Laval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A9_Laval "Université Laval") is the oldest post-secondary institution in Canada.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_BlakeKeshen2017p249-89) The largest university is the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto") with over 85,000 students.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-90) Four universities are regularly ranked among the top 100 world-wide, namely the University of Toronto, [University of British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_British_Columbia "University of British Columbia"), [McGill University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McGill_University "McGill University"), and [McMaster University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMaster_University "McMaster University"), with a total of [18 universities ranked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankings_of_universities_in_Canada "Rankings of universities in Canada") in the top 500 worldwide.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-91)

According to a 2022 report by the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD"), Canada is the most educated country in the world;[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_Statistics_Canada_2022_n626-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_OECD_2023_t514-93) the country ranks first worldwide in the percentage of adults having [tertiary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_education "Tertiary education"), with over 57 per cent of Canadian adults having attained at least an undergraduate college or university degree.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_Education_c106-94) Canada spends an average of about 5.3 per cent of its GDP on education.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_TheGlobalEconomy.com_1971_w626-95) The country invests heavily in tertiary education (more than US$20,000 per student).[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-96) As of 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit), 89 per cent of adults aged 25 to 64 have earned the equivalent of a high-school degree, compared to an OECD average of 75 per cent.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_OECD_2023_t514-93)

The [mandatory education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compulsory_education "Compulsory education") age ranges between 5–7 to 16–18 years,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-97) contributing to an adult literacy rate of 99 per cent.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_cia-98) Just over 60,000 children are [homeschooled in the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeschooling_in_Canada "Homeschooling in Canada") as of 2016. The [Programme for International Student Assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programme_for_International_Student_Assessment "Programme for International Student Assessment") indicates Canadian students perform well above the OECD average, particularly in mathematics, science, and reading,[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-100) ranking the overall knowledge and skills of Canadian 15-year-olds as the sixth-best in the world, although these scores have been declining in recent years. Canada is a well-performing OECD country in reading literacy, mathematics, and science, with the average student scoring 523.7, compared with the OECD average of 493 in 2015.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-102)

#### Healthcare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Healthcare")]

Main article: [Healthcare in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Canada "Healthcare in Canada")

This section is an excerpt from [Healthcare in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Canada "Healthcare in Canada").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Healthcare_in_Canada&action=edit)]

[Healthcare in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Canada "Healthcare in Canada") is delivered through the provincial and territorial systems of [publicly funded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publicly_funded_health_care "Publicly funded health care")[single-payer healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-payer_healthcare "Single-payer healthcare"), informally called [Medicare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(Canada) "Medicare (Canada)").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_AaseWaring2017-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-104) It is guided by the provisions of the _[Canada Health Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada\_Health\_Act "Canada Health Act"),_ adopted during 1984,[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_B%C3%A9gin1988-105) and is [universal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_LeattMapa2003-106):81 The 2002 [Royal Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Commission_on_the_Future_of_Health_Care_in_Canada "Royal Commission on the Future of Health Care in Canada"), known as the Romanow Report, revealed that Canadians consider universal access to publicly funded health services as a "fundamental value that ensures national health care insurance for everyone wherever they live in the country".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Romanow_Report_2002-107)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Romanow_Recommendations_2002-108)

Canadian Medicare provides coverage for approximately 70 percent of Canadians' healthcare needs, and the remaining 30 percent is paid for through the private sector.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_CIHI_2019-109)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_CIHI_2005-110) The 30 percent typically relates to services not covered or only partially covered by Medicare, such as [prescription drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prescription_drug "Prescription drug"), eye care, [medical devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_device "Medical device"), [gender care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender_health_care "Transgender health care"), [psychotherapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychotherapy "Psychotherapy"), [physical therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_therapy "Physical therapy") and [dentistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentistry_in_Canada "Dentistry in Canada").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_CIHI_2019-109)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_CIHI_2005-110) About 65-75 percent of Canadians have some form of supplementary [health insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_insurance "Health insurance") related to the aforementioned reasons; many receive it through their employers or use secondary [social programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_programs_in_Canada "Social programs in Canada") related to extended coverage for families receiving [social assistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_protection#Social_assistance "Social protection") or vulnerable demographics, such as seniors, minors, and those with disabilities.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_WaPo_20170701-111)

According to the [Canadian Institute for Health Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Institute_for_Health_Information "Canadian Institute for Health Information") (CIHI), by 2019, Canada's [aging population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aging_population "Aging population") represents an increase in healthcare costs of approximately one percent a year, which is a modest increase. In a 2020 [Statistics Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_Canada "Statistics Canada") Canadian Perspectives Survey Series (CPSS), 69 percent of Canadians self-reported that they had excellent or very good physical health—an improvement from 60 percent in 2018.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_statcan_Findlay_20200424-112) In 2019, 80 percent of Canadian adults self-reported having at least one major risk factor for chronic disease: [smoking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoking_in_Canada "Smoking in Canada"), physical inactivity, unhealthy eating, or excessive [alcohol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholic_drinks_in_Canada "Alcoholic drinks in Canada") use.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_GregoryStephens2019-113) Canada has [one of the highest rates of adult obesity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obesity_in_Canada "Obesity in Canada") among [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD") (OECD) countries attributing to approximately 2.7 million cases of [diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetes "Diabetes") (types 1 and 2 combined).[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_GregoryStephens2019-113) Four chronic diseases—[cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer "Cancer") (a leading cause of death), [cardiovascular diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular_disease "Cardiovascular disease"), [respiratory diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_disease "Respiratory disease") and diabetes account for 65 percent of deaths in Canada.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_GregoryStephens2019-113) There are approximately 8 million individuals aged 15 and older with one or more [disabilities in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability_in_Canada "Disability in Canada").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_k471-114)

In 2021, the [Canadian Institute for Health Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Institute_for_Health_Information "Canadian Institute for Health Information") reported that [healthcare spending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_spending_as_percent_of_gross_domestic_product_(GDP)_by_country "Health spending as percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by country") reached $308 billion, or 12.7 percent of Canada's GDP for that year.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-115) In 2022 Canada's per-capita spending on [health expenditures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_total_health_expenditure_per_capita "List of countries by total health expenditure per capita") ranked 12th among [healthcare systems in the OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_total_health_expenditure_per_capita "List of countries by total health expenditure per capita").[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_OECD-barcharts-116) Canada has performed close to the average on the majority of OECD health indicators since the early 2000s,[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-117) and ranks above average for [access to care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care"), but the number of doctors and hospital beds are considerably below the OECD average.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_OECD_2017-118) The [Commonwealth Funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Fund "Commonwealth Fund") 2021 report comparing the healthcare systems of 11 high-income countries ranked Canada second-to-last.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_auto3-119) Identified weaknesses of Canada's system were comparatively higher infant mortality rate, the prevalence of chronic conditions, long wait times, poor availability of after-hours care, and a lack of prescription drugs coverage.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Prescription_for_Canada-120) An increasing problem in Canada's health system is a shortage of [healthcare professionals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_professional "Health professional") and hospital capacity.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Duong_Vogel_2023_pp._E309%E2%80%93E310-121)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Thiessen_Partner_Organization_Ma_2023_j399-122)

#### Tourism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Tourism")]

Main article: [Tourism in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Canada "Tourism in Canada")

This section is an excerpt from [Tourism in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Canada "Tourism in Canada").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tourism_in_Canada&action=edit)]

[Tourism in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Canada "Tourism in Canada") is a major economic driver in the service sector, attracting millions of visitors and supporting approximately 10% of the national labor force. In recent years, statistics show that Canada has received over 20 million international tourists annually.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_n066-123) The summer months are especially popular for travellers both domestically and internationally.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_l240-124) Tourism and supporting industries contributed over $100 billion to the Canadian national economy in 2024. The sector supports nearly 1.8 million Canadians working in tourism-related fields.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_n066-123)

Domestic tourism in Canada is the principal economic driver of the sector, with statistics indicating that, in 2024, about 70% of all tourism spending came from Canadian residents exploring their own country.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_n066-123) Domestic statistics also indicate that travel within provinces is prevalent, with residents supporting local businesses and attractions.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_n066-123)[Land border crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Canada%E2%80%93United_States_border_crossings "List of Canada–United States border crossings") by United States citizens has historically been the largest source of inbound tourists, followed by [international airline travel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_international_airports_in_Canada "List of international airports in Canada") from the United Kingdom and other European countries.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_f677-125) Visitors from Asia have become more popular in recent decades.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_l299-126) Passport holders from over 50 visa-exempt countries and nationals who require a visa can visit Canada for up to six months at a time.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_r896-127)

Federal, provincial, municipal and local government initiatives aimed at promoting sustainable tourism and attracting foreign tourists play a major role in the industry.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_u976-128) Canada is known for its safety and security,[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Tourism_in_Canada_k500-129) attracting tourists through its natural features (e.g., [Niagara Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls "Niagara Falls")), [festivals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_festivals_in_Canada "List of festivals in Canada") (e.g., [Calgary stampede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary_stampede "Calgary stampede")), [arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_art "Canadian art") (e.g., [Toronto International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_International_Film_Festival "Toronto International Film Festival")), [heritage sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Canada "List of World Heritage Sites in Canada"), (e.g., [Quebec city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_city "Quebec city")) sporting events (e.g.,[Grey Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey_Cup "Grey Cup")), amusement parks (e.g., [Canada's Wonderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada's_Wonderland "Canada's Wonderland")) and its diverse culture (e.g., [Caribbean Carnival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribana "Caribana")).

### Manufacturing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Manufacturing")]

Main pages: [Technological and industrial history of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technological_and_industrial_history_of_Canada "Technological and industrial history of Canada") and [Category:Manufacturing in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Manufacturing_in_Canada "Category:Manufacturing in Canada")

[![Image 40](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Ford_Oakville_Assembly.JPG/250px-Ford_Oakville_Assembly.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ford_Oakville_Assembly.JPG)

[Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Motor_Company "Ford Motor Company")'s [Oakville Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakville_Assembly "Oakville Assembly") in the [Greater Toronto Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Toronto_Area "Greater Toronto Area"). Central Canada is home to several auto factories of the major American and Japanese automakers.

The [general pattern of development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-sector_model "Three-sector model") for wealthy nations was a transition from a raw material production-based economy to a manufacturing-based economy and then to a service-based economy. At its World War II peak in 1944, Canada's manufacturing sector accounted for 29% of GDP,[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-mfggdp-135) declining to 10.37% in 2017.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-industry_GDP-67) Canada has not suffered as greatly as most other rich, industrialized nations from the pains of the relative decline in the importance of manufacturing since the 1960s.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-mfggdp-135) A 2009 study by [Statistics Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_Canada "Statistics Canada") also found that, while manufacturing declined as a relative percentage of GDP from 24.3% in the 1960s to 15.6% in 2005, manufacturing volumes between 1961 and 2005 kept pace with the overall growth in the volume index of GDP.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-136) Manufacturing in Canada declined significantly during the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"). As of 2017, manufacturing accounts for 10% of Canada's GDP,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-industry_GDP-67) a relative decline of more than 5% of GDP since 2005.

Central Canada is home to [branch plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branch_plant "Branch plant") to all the major American and Japanese automobile makers and many parts factories owned by Canadian firms such as [Magna International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_International "Magna International") and [Linamar Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linamar "Linamar").

#### Automotive

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Automotive")]

Main article: [Automotive industry in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_industry_in_Canada "Automotive industry in Canada")

This section is an excerpt from [Automotive industry in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_industry_in_Canada "Automotive industry in Canada").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Automotive_industry_in_Canada&action=edit)]

The [automotive industry in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_industry_in_Canada "Automotive industry in Canada") consists primarily of assembly plants of foreign [automakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_industry "Automotive industry"), most with headquarters in the United States or Japan, along with hundreds of manufacturers of [automotive parts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_auto_parts "List of auto parts") and systems.

Canada is currently the [thirteenth-largest auto-producing nation in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_motor_vehicle_production "List of countries by motor vehicle production"), and seventh largest auto exporter by value, producing 1.4 million vehicles and exporting $32 billion worth of vehicles in 2020.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-137) Canada's highest rankings ever were the second-largest producer in the world between 1918 and 1923 and third-largest after World War II.

Automotive manufacturing is one of Canada's largest industrial sectors, accounting for 10% of manufacturing GDP and 23% of manufacturing trade. Canada produces passenger vehicles, trucks and buses, auto parts and systems, truck bodies and trailers, as well as tires and machine, tools, dies and molds (MTDM). The auto industry directly employs more than 125,000 people in vehicle assembly and auto parts manufacturing, and another 380,000 in distribution and aftermarket sales and service.

#### Steel

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Steel")]

[![Image 41](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ea/HamiltonNorthEndIndustrialA.JPG/250px-HamiltonNorthEndIndustrialA.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HamiltonNorthEndIndustrialA.JPG)

[ArcelorMittal Dofasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dofasco "Dofasco"), view from Burlington Street

Canada was the world's nineteenth-largest steel exporter in 2018. In year-to-date 2019 (through March), further referred to as YTD 2019, Canada exported 1.39 million metric tons of steel, a 22 percent decrease from 1.79 million metric tons in YTD 2018. Based on available data, Canada's exports represented about 1.5 percent of all steel exported globally in 2017. By volume, Canada's 2018 steel exports represented just over one-tenth the volume of the world's largest exporter, China. In value terms, steel represented 1.4 percent of the total goods Canada exported in 2018. The growth in exports in the decade since 2009 has been 29%. The largest producers in 2018 were [ArcelorMittal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ArcelorMittal "ArcelorMittal"), [Essar Steel Algoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essar_Steel_Algoma "Essar Steel Algoma"), and the first of those alone accounted for roughly half of Canadian steel production through its two subsidiaries. The top two markets for Canada's exports were its [NAFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAFTA "NAFTA") partners, and by themselves accounted for 92 percent of exports by volume. Canada sent 83 percent of its steel exports to the United States in YTD 2019. The gap between domestic demand and domestic production increased to −2.4 million metric tons, up from −0.2 million metric tons in YTD 2018. In YTD 2019, exports as a share of production decreased to 41.6 percent from 53 percent in YTD 2018.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-usdoc-139)

In 2017, [heavy industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_industry "Heavy industry") accounted for 10.2% of Canada's greenhouse gas emissions.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-:1-140)

#### Electricity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Electricity")]

Main article: [Electricity sector in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity_sector_in_Canada "Electricity sector in Canada")

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Canada_electricity_generation_by_source.png/250px-Canada_electricity_generation_by_source.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Canada_electricity_generation_by_source.png)

Share of electricity generation in Canada – percentage share

The [electricity sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity_sector "Electricity sector") in [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") has played a significant role in the economic and political life of the country since the late 19th century. The sector is organized along provincial and territorial lines. In a majority of provinces, large [government-owned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government-owned_company "Government-owned company") integrated public utilities play a leading role in the [generation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity_generation "Electricity generation"), [transmission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_power_transmission "Electric power transmission") and [distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_power_distribution "Electric power distribution") of electricity. [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") and [Alberta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberta "Alberta") have created [electricity markets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity_market "Electricity market") in the last decade in order to increase investment and competition in this sector of the economy. In 2017, the electricity sector accounted for 10% of total national greenhouse gas emissions.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-:0-163) Canada has substantial electricity trade with the neighbouring [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") amounting to 72 TWh exports and 10 TWh imports in 2017.

[Hydroelectricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydroelectricity "Hydroelectricity") accounted for 59% of all electric generation in Canada in 2016,[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-164) making Canada the world's second-largest producer of hydroelectricity after China.[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-165) Since 1960, large hydroelectric projects, especially in [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec"), [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"), [Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoba "Manitoba") and [Newfoundland and Labrador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newfoundland_and_Labrador "Newfoundland and Labrador"), have significantly increased the country's generation capacity.

The second-largest single source of power (15% of the total) is nuclear power, with several plants in Ontario generating more than half of that province's electricity and one generator in [New Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_Lepreau_Nuclear_Generating_Station "Point Lepreau Nuclear Generating Station"). This makes Canada the world's sixth-largest electricity producer generated by nuclear power, producing 95 TWh in 2017.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-166)

Fossil fuels provide 19% of Canadian electric power, about half as coal (9% of the total), and the remainder a mix of natural gas and oil. Only five provinces use coal for electricity generation. Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Nova Scotia rely on coal for nearly half of their generation, while other provinces and territories use little or none. Alberta and Saskatchewan also use a substantial amount of natural gas. Remote communities, including all of Nunavut and much of the Northwest Territories, produce most of their electricity from diesel generators at high economic and environmental costs. The federal government has set up initiatives to reduce dependence on diesel-fired electricity.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-167)

Non-hydro renewables are a fast-growing portion of the total, at 7% in 2016.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

#### Oil and gas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Oil and gas")]

Main articles: [Petroleum industry in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_industry_in_Canada "Petroleum industry in Canada"), [Fracking in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fracking_in_Canada "Fracking in Canada"), and [Pipelines in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipelines_in_Canada "Pipelines in Canada")

See also: [History of the petroleum industry in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_petroleum_industry_in_Canada "History of the petroleum industry in Canada")

[![Image 43](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/SyncrudeWoodBuffalo.JPG/250px-SyncrudeWoodBuffalo.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SyncrudeWoodBuffalo.JPG)

[Syncrude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncrude "Syncrude")'s Mildred Lake plant site at the [Athabasca oil sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athabasca_oil_sands "Athabasca oil sands") in [Alberta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberta "Alberta")

Canada possesses extensive oil and gas resources centred in Alberta, and the Northern Territories but is also present in neighboring [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia") and [Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan "Saskatchewan"). The vast [Athabasca oil sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athabasca_oil_sands "Athabasca oil sands") give Canada the world's third-largest reserves of oil after Saudi Arabia and Venezuela, according to [USGS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USGS "USGS"). The oil and gas industry represents 27% of Canada's total [greenhouse gas emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions"), an increase of 84% since 1990, mostly due to the development of the oil sands.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-:0-163)

Historically, an important issue in Canadian politics is the interplay between the oil and energy industry in [Western Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Canada "Western Canada") and the industrial heartland of Southern Ontario. Foreign investment in Western oil projects has fueled [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada")'s rising dollar. This has raised the price of Ontario's manufacturing exports and made them less competitive, a problem similar to the [decline of the manufacturing sector in the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_disease "Dutch disease").[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-168)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-169)

The [National Energy Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Energy_Policy "National Energy Policy") of the early 1980s attempted to make Canada oil-sufficient and to ensure equal supply and price of oil in all parts of Canada, especially for the eastern manufacturing base.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-canadian_eclopedia-170) This policy proved deeply divisive as it forced Alberta to sell low-priced oil to eastern Canada.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-National_Post_2012-171) The policy was eliminated 5 years after it was first announced amid a collapse of oil prices in 1985. The new Prime Minister [Brian Mulroney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Mulroney "Brian Mulroney") had campaigned against the policy in the [1984 Canadian federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Canadian_federal_election "1984 Canadian federal election"). One of the most controversial sections of the [Canada–United States Free Trade Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93United_States_Free_Trade_Agreement "Canada–United States Free Trade Agreement") of 1988 was a promise that Canada would never charge the United States more for energy than fellow Canadians.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-:1-140)

### Agriculture, fishing, livestock and forestry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Agriculture, fishing, livestock and forestry")]

Main articles: [Agriculture in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture_in_Canada "Agriculture in Canada"), [Aquaculture in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquaculture_in_Canada "Aquaculture in Canada"), [Dairy farming in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dairy_farming_in_Canada "Dairy farming in Canada"), [Fishing industry in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing_industry_in_Canada "Fishing industry in Canada"), and [Forestry in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forestry_in_Canada "Forestry in Canada")

See also: [Dairy and poultry supply management in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dairy_and_poultry_supply_management_in_Canada "Dairy and poultry supply management in Canada")

[![Image 44](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/InlandGrainTerminal.jpg/250px-InlandGrainTerminal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:InlandGrainTerminal.jpg)

An inland grain terminal along the [Yellowhead Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowhead_Highway "Yellowhead Highway") in [Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan "Saskatchewan")

Canada is one of the world's largest suppliers of agricultural products, particularly wheat and other grains.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-172) Canada is a major exporter of agricultural products, to the United States and Asia. As with all other developed nations, the proportion of the population and GDP devoted to agriculture fell dramatically over the 20th century. The agriculture and agri-food manufacturing sector created $49.0 billion to Canada's GDP in 2015, accounting for 2.6% of total GDP.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-173) This sector also accounts for 8.4% of Canada's Greenhouse gas emissions.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-:1-140)

The Canadian agriculture industry receives significant government subsidies and support as with other developed nations.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-174) However, Canada has strongly supported reducing market influencing subsidies through the [World Trade Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Organization "World Trade Organization").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 2000, Canada spent approximately CDN$4.6 billion on support for the industry.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] $2.32 billion was classified under the WTO designation of "green box" license, meaning it did not directly influence the market, such as money for research or disaster relief.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] All but $848.2 million were subsidies worth less than 5% of the value of the crops they were provided for.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Transportation")]

Main article: [Transportation in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Canada "Transportation in Canada")

See also: [Roads in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roads_in_Canada "Roads in Canada"), [List of Canadian railways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Canadian_railways "List of Canadian railways"), [List of airports in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_airports_in_Canada "List of airports in Canada"), [List of airlines of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_airlines_of_Canada "List of airlines of Canada"), and [Category:Ports and harbours of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Ports_and_harbours_of_Canada "Category:Ports and harbours of Canada")

This section is an excerpt from [Transportation in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_in_Canada "Transportation in Canada").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Transportation_in_Canada&action=edit)]

Canada, the world's [second-largest country in total area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area "List of countries and dependencies by area"), is dedicated to having efficient, high-capacity multimodal [transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation "Transportation") spanning often vast distances between [natural resource extraction sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Canada "Geography of Canada"), [agricultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture_in_Canada "Agriculture in Canada") and [urban areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_census_metropolitan_areas_and_agglomerations_in_Canada "List of census metropolitan areas and agglomerations in Canada"). Canada's transportation system includes more than 1,400,000 kilometres (870,000 mi) of roads, 10 major international airports, 300 smaller airports, 72,093 km (44,797 mi) of functioning railway track, and more than 300 commercial ports and harbours that provide access to the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean"), [Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") and [Arctic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_Ocean "Arctic Ocean") oceans as well as the [Great Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes "Great Lakes") and the [St. Lawrence Seaway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Lawrence_Seaway "St. Lawrence Seaway").[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-175) In 2005, the transportation sector made up 4.2% of Canada's GDP, compared to 3.7% for Canada's mining and oil and gas extraction industries.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Transportation_in_Canada_Trans_Sector_05-176)

[Transport Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Canada "Transport Canada") oversees and regulates most aspects of transportation within federal jurisdiction, including interprovincial transport. This primarily includes rail, air and maritime transportation. Transport Canada is under the direction of the federal government's [Minister of Transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Transport_(Canada) "Minister of Transport (Canada)"). The [Transportation Safety Board of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transportation_Safety_Board_of_Canada "Transportation Safety Board of Canada") is responsible for maintaining transportation safety in Canada by investigating accidents and making safety recommendations.

[Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") has an advanced and diversified [mixed economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_economy "Mixed economy"). The nation relies upon its [abundant natural resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Canada#Natural_resources "Geography of Canada") and well-developed [international trade networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_largest_trading_partners_of_Canada "List of the largest trading partners of Canada").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-econ-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-32) As of 2026, it is the [eleventh-largest in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) "List of countries by GDP (nominal)") in nominal terms. Its [GDP per capita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP_per_capita "GDP per capita") in [purchasing power parity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity") (PPP) terms ranks third among G7 countries.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-World_Bank-7)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-33) Among OECD members, Canada has a highly efficient and strong [social security system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_programs_in_Canada "Social programs in Canada"); social expenditure stood at [roughly 23.1% of GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welfare_state#Effects "Welfare state"). The country's average household [disposable income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disposable_income "Disposable income") per capita is "well above" the OECD average.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-34) The [Government of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Canada "Government of Canada") formulates economic policy while the [Bank of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Canada "Bank of Canada") functions as its [central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank "Central bank") and implements monetary policy.

The Canadian economy ranks low in [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_in_Canada "Corruption in Canada") and [income disparity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_inequality "Economic inequality") while ranking highly on economic freedom and stability.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-cpi-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-36) Canada ranks among the lowest of the most developed countries for [housing affordability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_housing_in_Canada "Affordable housing in Canada").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-37) It maintains a highly developed banking sector with the [Toronto Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Stock_Exchange "Toronto Stock Exchange") ranked the [tenth-largest stock exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_stock_exchanges "List of stock exchanges") in the world by [market capitalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-38) Its [cooperative banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative_banking "Cooperative banking") sector is pronounced with the world's highest per-capita membership in [credit unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_union "Credit union").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-39) Among [G20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G20 "G20") members, Canada has the second-largest [foreign direct investment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_direct_investment "Foreign direct investment") to GDP ratio and the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio in the G7.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-w479-40)

## Contemporary era overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Contemporary era overview")]

Main article: [Economic history of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_history_of_Canada "Economic history of Canada")

Since the early 20th century, the growth of Canada's manufacturing, mining, and service sectors has transformed the nation from a largely rural economy to an urbanized, industrial one.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-41) The Canadian economy is dominated by the [service industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_sector_of_the_economy "Tertiary sector of the economy"), which employs about three-quarters of the country's workforce.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-42) Among developed countries, Canada has an unusually important [primary sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_sector_of_the_economy "Primary sector of the economy"), of which the [forestry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forestry_in_Canada "Forestry in Canada") and [petroleum industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum_industry_in_Canada "Petroleum industry in Canada") are the most prominent components.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-SueyoshiGoto2018-43) Many towns in northern Canada, where agriculture is difficult, are sustained by nearby mines or sources of timber.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-44) Canada spends [around 1.70% of GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_by_research_and_development_spending "List of sovereign states by research and development spending") on advanced [research and development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_and_development "Research and development") across various sectors of the economy.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-unctad-46)

Canada's economic integration with the United States has increased significantly since [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-47) The [Automotive Products Trade Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_Products_Trade_Agreement "Automotive Products Trade Agreement") of 1965 opened Canada's borders to trade in the automobile manufacturing industry.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-48) In the 1970s, concerns over energy self-sufficiency and foreign ownership in the manufacturing sectors prompted the federal government to enact the [National Energy Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Energy_Program "National Energy Program") (NEP) and the [Foreign Investment Review Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Investment_Review_Agency "Foreign Investment Review Agency") (FIRA).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-49) The government abolished the NEP in the 1980s and changed the name of FIRA to [Invest in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invest_in_Canada "Invest in Canada") to encourage foreign investment.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-50) The [Canada– United States Free Trade Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_%E2%80%93_United_States_Free_Trade_Agreement "Canada – United States Free Trade Agreement") (FTA) of 1988 eliminated tariffs between the two countries, while the [North American Free Trade Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Free_Trade_Agreement "North American Free Trade Agreement") (NAFTA) expanded the free-trade zone to include [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico") in 1994 (later replaced by the [Canada–United States–Mexico Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States%E2%80%93Mexico%E2%80%93Canada_Agreement "United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement")).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-51) As of 2023, [Canada is a signatory to 15 free trade agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade_agreements_of_Canada "Free trade agreements of Canada") with 51 countries.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-GAC_2020-52)

Canada is one of the few developed nations that are net exporters of energy.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-SueyoshiGoto2018-43)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-53)[Atlantic Canada possesses vast offshore deposits of natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offshore_drilling_in_Atlantic_Canada "Offshore drilling in Atlantic Canada"),[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-54) and Alberta hosts the fourth-largest oil reserves in the world.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Monga_2022-55) The vast [Athabasca oil sands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athabasca_oil_sands "Athabasca oil sands") and other oil reserves give Canada 13% of global oil reserves, constituting the [world's third or fourth-largest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_proven_oil_reserves "List of countries by proven oil reserves").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-56) Canada is additionally one of the world's largest suppliers of [agricultural products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture_in_Canada "Agriculture in Canada"); the [Canadian Prairies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Prairies "Canadian Prairies") are one of the most important global producers of wheat, [canola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canola "Canola"), and other grains.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-57) The [country is a leading exporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_exports_of_Canada "List of exports of Canada") of zinc, uranium, gold, nickel, [platinoids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_group "Platinum group"), aluminum, steel, [iron ore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_ore "Iron ore"), [coking coal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coking_coal "Coking coal"), lead, copper, molybdenum, cobalt, and cadmium.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-OEC_-_The_Observatory_of_Economic_Complexity-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-The_Atlas_of_Economic_Complexity-59) Canada has a sizeable heavy manufacturing sector centred in southern Ontario and Quebec, with automobiles and [aeronautics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeronautics "Aeronautics") representing particularly important industries.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-60) The [country's fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing_industry_in_Canada "Fishing industry in Canada") and [tourism industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Canada "Tourism in Canada") are also key contributors to the economy.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-61)

## Monetary policy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Monetary policy")]

The mandate of the central bank—the [Bank of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Canada "Bank of Canada")—is to conduct monetary policy that manages [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation "Inflation") to ensure the Canadian dollar's long-term [purchasing power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchasing_power "Purchasing power").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Monetary_Policy_Report_2015_07-63)

Under the [inflation-targeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation_targeting "Inflation targeting") monetary policy that has been the cornerstone of Canada's monetary and fiscal policy since the early 1990s, the Bank of Canada sets an inflation target.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Monetary_Policy_Report_2015_07-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-inflation-targeting_2010-64) The inflation target was set at 2%, which is the midpoint of an inflation range of 1 to 3%. They established a set of inflation-reduction targets to keep inflation "low, stable and predictable" and to foster Canada's sustained economic growth, employment gains and improved standard of living.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Monetary_Policy_Report_2015_07-63)

Following the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession "Great Recession"), the narrow focus of inflation-targeting as a means of providing stable growth in the Canadian economy was revised.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-beyond_inflation-targeting_2011-65) By 2011, the then-Bank of Canada Governor [Mark Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Carney "Mark Carney") argued that monetary policy would allow for a more flexible inflation-targeting in specific situations, specifically those favorable to employment or economic gains.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-beyond_inflation-targeting_2011-65)

The Bank of Canada reassessed their mandate 15 years later in 2026 in response to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Canada "COVID-19 pandemic in Canada") and a [trade war with the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%932026_United_States_trade_war_with_Canada "2025–2026 United States trade war with Canada").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-:10-66) Their framework was adjusted to prioritize reducing inflation, rising housing costs, and protection against [supply shocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supply_shock "Supply shock").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-:10-66)

Canada's real estate market is the backbone of the economy, comprising over 13% of the GDP by sector in 2024. In 2024, housing investment accounted for 25% of national wealth,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-68) up from 21% in 2021.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-69) It is difficult to discern the actual contribution of other sectors (such as construction, Investment and financial services, manufacturing, and forestry) to real estate, rental and leasing, as these industries are intrinsically linked in a complex economy. The Bank of Canada has increased its mortgage bond holdings to target 50% of the fixed-rate primary issuances.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-70)

### Service sector

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Service sector")]

See also: [Category:Service industries in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Service_industries_in_Canada "Category:Service industries in Canada")

The service sector in Canada is vast and multifaceted, employing about three quarters of Canadians and accounting for 70% of GDP.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-auto-72) The largest employer is the [retail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail "Retail") sector, employing almost 12% of Canadians.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-73) The retail industry is concentrated mainly in a small number of chain stores clustered together in [shopping malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shopping_mall "Shopping mall"). In recent years, there has been an increase in the number of [big-box stores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big-box_store "Big-box store"), such as [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart "Walmart") (of the United States), [Real Canadian Superstore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Canadian_Superstore "Real Canadian Superstore"), and [Best Buy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Buy "Best Buy") (of the United States). This has led to fewer workers in this sector and the migration of retail jobs to the suburbs.

[![Image 35](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Vancouver_downtown.jpg/250px-Vancouver_downtown.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vancouver_downtown.jpg)

The [Financial District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_District,_Vancouver "Financial District, Vancouver") in [Downtown Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Vancouver "Downtown Vancouver"). Canadian business services are largely concentrated in large urban areas of Canada.

The second-largest portion of the service sector is the business service, and it employs only a slightly smaller percentage of the population.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-74) This includes [financial services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_services "Financial services"), [real estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate "Real estate"), and communications industries. This portion of the economy has been rapidly growing in recent years. It is largely concentrated in the major urban centres, especially [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal") and [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver").

The education and health sectors are two of Canada's largest, but both are primarily under the influence of the government. The health care industry has been quickly growing and is the third-largest in Canada.

Canada has an important [high tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_tech "High tech") industry,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-75) and a burgeoning film, television, and entertainment industry creating content for local and international consumption (see [Media in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_in_Canada "Media in Canada")).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-76)[Tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism_in_Canada "Tourism in Canada") attracts millions of visitors and supports approximately 10% of the national labor force. In recent years, statistics show that Canada has received over 20 million international tourists annually.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-n066-77) The summer months are especially popular for travelers both domestically and internationally.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-l240-78) Tourism and supporting industries contributed over $100 billion to the Canadian national economy in 2024. The sector supports nearly 1.8 million Canadians working in tourism-related fields.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-n066-77)

The banking sector of [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") is a large component of the [nation's private sector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_companies_of_Canada "List of companies of Canada") and the broader Canadian economy. It is dominated by a small number of large banks, with the six largest combining for 93% of the banking assets.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-79) The two largest, the [Royal Bank of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Bank_of_Canada "Royal Bank of Canada") and the [Toronto Dominion Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Dominion_Bank "Toronto Dominion Bank") are among the world's 25 largest banks.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Banking_in_Canada_SP-80) It has been considered to be one of the safest and soundest banking systems in the world.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Banking_in_Canada_WEF-81)

Canada's banks have high service levels and investments in technology. A report released by the office of the [Minister of Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_Finance_(Canada) "Minister of Finance (Canada)") in 2002 states "Canada has the highest number of ATMs per capita in the world and benefits from the highest penetration levels of electronic channels such as [debit cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debit_cards "Debit cards"), [Internet banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_banking "Internet banking") and [telephone banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephone_banking "Telephone banking")".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Banking_in_Canada_fingcca-82) More recent data published by the [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") shows that as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit) Canada has 227.82 ATMs per 100,000 adults, which ranks the country third worldwide.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-83)

[Education in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Canada "Education in Canada") is for the most part provided [publicly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_school "State school"), funded and overseen by [federal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Canada "Government of Canada"), [provincial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_and_territories_of_Canada "Provinces and territories of Canada"), and [local governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_government "Local government").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-84) Education is within provincial jurisdiction and the curriculum is overseen by the province.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-85)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-86) Education in Canada is generally divided into [primary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_education "Primary education"), followed by secondary education and post-secondary. Education in both English and French is available in most places across Canada.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-87) Canada has a large number of universities, almost all of which are publicly funded.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-88) Established in 1663, [Université Laval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A9_Laval "Université Laval") is the oldest post-secondary institution in Canada.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_BlakeKeshen2017p249-89) The largest university is the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto "University of Toronto") with over 85,000 students.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-90) Four universities are regularly ranked among the top 100 world-wide, namely the University of Toronto, [University of British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_British_Columbia "University of British Columbia"), [McGill University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McGill_University "McGill University"), and [McMaster University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMaster_University "McMaster University"), with a total of [18 universities ranked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rankings_of_universities_in_Canada "Rankings of universities in Canada") in the top 500 worldwide.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-91)

According to a 2022 report by the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD"), Canada is the most educated country in the world;[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_Statistics_Canada_2022_n626-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_OECD_2023_t514-93) the country ranks first worldwide in the percentage of adults having [tertiary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_education "Tertiary education"), with over 57 per cent of Canadian adults having attained at least an undergraduate college or university degree.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_Education_c106-94) Canada spends an average of about 5.3 per cent of its GDP on education.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_TheGlobalEconomy.com_1971_w626-95) The country invests heavily in tertiary education (more than US$20,000 per student).[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-96) As of 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit), 89 per cent of adults aged 25 to 64 have earned the equivalent of a high-school degree, compared to an OECD average of 75 per cent.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_OECD_2023_t514-93)

The [mandatory education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compulsory_education "Compulsory education") age ranges between 5–7 to 16–18 years,[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-97) contributing to an adult literacy rate of 99 per cent.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Education_in_Canada_cia-98) Just over 60,000 children are [homeschooled in the country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeschooling_in_Canada "Homeschooling in Canada") as of 2016. The [Programme for International Student Assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programme_for_International_Student_Assessment "Programme for International Student Assessment") indicates Canadian students perform well above the OECD average, particularly in mathematics, science, and reading,[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-99)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-100) ranking the overall knowledge and skills of Canadian 15-year-olds as the sixth-best in the world, although these scores have been declining in recent years. Canada is a well-performing OECD country in reading literacy, mathematics, and science, with the average student scoring 523.7, compared with the OECD average of 493 in 2015.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-101)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-102)

#### Healthcare

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Economy_of_Canada&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Healthcare")]

Main article: [Healthcare in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Canada "Healthcare in Canada")

This section is an excerpt from [Healthcare in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Canada "Healthcare in Canada").[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Healthcare_in_Canada&action=edit)]

[Healthcare in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_in_Canada "Healthcare in Canada") is delivered through the provincial and territorial systems of [publicly funded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publicly_funded_health_care "Publicly funded health care")[single-payer healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-payer_healthcare "Single-payer healthcare"), informally called [Medicare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(Canada) "Medicare (Canada)").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_AaseWaring2017-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-104) It is guided by the provisions of the _[Canada Health Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada\_Health\_Act "Canada Health Act"),_ adopted during 1984,[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_B%C3%A9gin1988-105) and is [universal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_LeattMapa2003-106):81 The 2002 [Royal Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Commission_on_the_Future_of_Health_Care_in_Canada "Royal Commission on the Future of Health Care in Canada"), known as the Romanow Report, revealed that Canadians consider universal access to publicly funded health services as a "fundamental value that ensures national health care insurance for everyone wherever they live in the country".[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Romanow_Report_2002-107)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Romanow_Recommendations_2002-108)

Canadian Medicare provides coverage for approximately 70 percent of Canadians' healthcare needs, and the remaining 30 percent is paid for through the private sector.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_CIHI_2019-109)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_CIHI_2005-110) The 30 percent typically relates to services not covered or only partially covered by Medicare, such as [prescription drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prescription_drug "Prescription drug"), eye care, [medical devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_device "Medical device"), [gender care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender_health_care "Transgender health care"), [psychotherapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychotherapy "Psychotherapy"), [physical therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_therapy "Physical therapy") and [dentistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentistry_in_Canada "Dentistry in Canada").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_CIHI_2019-109)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_CIHI_2005-110) About 65-75 percent of Canadians have some form of supplementary [health insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_insurance "Health insurance") related to the aforementioned reasons; many receive it through their employers or use secondary [social programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_programs_in_Canada "Social programs in Canada") related to extended coverage for families receiving [social assistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_protection#Social_assistance "Social protection") or vulnerable demographics, such as seniors, minors, and those with disabilities.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_WaPo_20170701-111)

According to the [Canadian Institute for Health Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Institute_for_Health_Information "Canadian Institute for Health Information") (CIHI), by 2019, Canada's [aging population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aging_population "Aging population") represents an increase in healthcare costs of approximately one percent a year, which is a modest increase. In a 2020 [Statistics Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_Canada "Statistics Canada") Canadian Perspectives Survey Series (CPSS), 69 percent of Canadians self-reported that they had excellent or very good physical health—an improvement from 60 percent in 2018.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_statcan_Findlay_20200424-112) In 2019, 80 percent of Canadian adults self-reported having at least one major risk factor for chronic disease: [smoking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoking_in_Canada "Smoking in Canada"), physical inactivity, unhealthy eating, or excessive [alcohol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholic_drinks_in_Canada "Alcoholic drinks in Canada") use.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_GregoryStephens2019-113) Canada has [one of the highest rates of adult obesity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obesity_in_Canada "Obesity in Canada") among [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD") (OECD) countries attributing to approximately 2.7 million cases of [diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetes "Diabetes") (types 1 and 2 combined).[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_GregoryStephens2019-113) Four chronic diseases—[cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer "Cancer") (a leading cause of death), [cardiovascular diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular_disease "Cardiovascular disease"), [respiratory diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respiratory_disease "Respiratory disease") and diabetes account for 65 percent of deaths in Canada.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_GregoryStephens2019-113) There are approximately 8 million individuals aged 15 and older with one or more [disabilities in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability_in_Canada "Disability in Canada").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_k471-114)

In 2021, the [Canadian Institute for Health Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Institute_for_Health_Information "Canadian Institute for Health Information") reported that [healthcare spending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_spending_as_percent_of_gross_domestic_product_(GDP)_by_country "Health spending as percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by country") reached $308 billion, or 12.7 percent of Canada's GDP for that year.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-115) In 2022 Canada's per-capita spending on [health expenditures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_total_health_expenditure_per_capita "List of countries by total health expenditure per capita") ranked 12th among [healthcare systems in the OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_total_health_expenditure_per_capita "List of countries by total health expenditure per capita").[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_OECD-barcharts-116) Canada has performed close to the average on the majority of OECD health indicators since the early 2000s,[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-117) and ranks above average for [access to care](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_health_care "Universal health care"), but the number of doctors and hospital beds are considerably below the OECD average.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_OECD_2017-118) The [Commonwealth Funds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Fund "Commonwealth Fund") 2021 report comparing the healthcare systems of 11 high-income countries ranked Canada second-to-last.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_auto3-119) Identified weaknesses of Canada's system were comparatively higher infant mortality rate, the prevalence of chronic conditions, long wait times, poor availability of after-hours care, and a lack of prescription drugs coverage.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Prescription_for_Canada-120) An increasing problem in Canada's health system is a shortage of [healthcare professionals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_professional "Health professional") and hospital capacity.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Duong_Vogel_2023_pp._E309%E2%80%93E310-121)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_Canada#cite_note-Healthcare_in_Canada_Thiessen_Partner_Organization_Ma_2023_j399-122)
